title: Water Availability and Water Security
text:
← Back to Research
Studying how glacier-driven changes in water availability and reliability affect water security.
So far, we have focused on simulating long-term changes in mountain water resources and identifying potential tipping points. These are moments when a relatively stable water system could shift into a less reliable state. As glaciers shrink and snow cover declines, they may lose their ability to store water and release it during dry periods. Water supplies could then become less reliable.
But what would this mean for the people who rely on these rivers?
In this part of the project, we will explore how changes in freshwater availability could affect communities in the Vilcanota and Santa catchments. We will look at where water supplies may become less reliable, who depends on them, and what makes some communities more vulnerable than others.

title: Water Availability and Water Security
text:
Understanding the risk
A change in river flow does not affect everyone in the same way. Its consequences depend on three connected factors: hazard, exposure, and vulnerability.
Hazard: How likely is water availability to become unreliable?
Our Tipping Point Analysis will help us assess the likelihood of crossing a freshwater tipping point. We will describe this likelihood as low, medium, or high.
Exposure: Who and what depends on this water?
We will identify the people, livelihoods, and ecosystems that rely on these water resources, including communities using river water for drinking, farming, and other daily needs.
Vulnerability: How difficult would it be to cope with a change?
Some communities have more options than others when water becomes scarce. We will use a Social Vulnerability Index to bring together information about people’s water needs, their access to water, and their ability to cope with shortages as glaciers continue to shrink.
Together, these three factors will help us understand where changing water supplies could cause the greatest difficulties and where adaptation efforts may be most needed.

title: Water Availability and Water Security
text:
Finding ways forward
The loss of glaciers presents serious challenges. But understanding these changes can also help communities prepare, adapt, and find new ways to manage water.
We will explore opportunities for positive change alongside the risks. These could include fairer ways to share water, stronger cooperation between water users, and renewed support for ancestral knowledge and water management practices.
Our aim goes beyond identifying whether and when a tipping point might occur. We also want to ask: What comes next? By connecting changes in the rivers with people’s needs and experiences, we hope to support practical adaptation planning.

title: Tipping Rivers
text:
The Tipping Rivers project explores how glacier loss affects water security in mountain regions. As glaciers rapidly retreat due to climate change, we want to understand how these changes alter river flows, water availability, water quality, and ecosystems. A key focus of the project is to identify whether glacier retreat could push regions beyond critical tipping points, causing long-lasting changes of water resources mountain communities depend on.
We will compare two case study sites that are experiencing rapid glacier retreat and increasing uncertainty in future water security. Research suggests that these regions have already past the hydrological tipping point of ‘peak water’, which marks the transition from increasing to decreasing melt water supply. We want to know if this transition also represents a tipping point for water security or whether catchment processes and water-management systems provide resilience that can buffer the impacts of declining glacier melt water.

From September 2026 to August 2028, this website will be regularly updated with news about project progress, the data collected and created, fieldwork stories, and, a few exciting publications. So, feel invited to come back anytime to check-out our updates and new resources.

title: Data and Evidence
section: What data do we collect and generate?
text:
What data do we collect and generate?
Combining historical records, field measurements, and computer models, we will reconstruct changes from 1850 to today in:

River flow: how much water moves through rivers, across seasons and years.
Soil moisture: how much water remains in the ground.
Evaporation and plant water use: how much water returns from the land to the atmosphere.
Vegetation: how do plant growth and leaf cover change and how does this influence water availability.
Water quality: how does water quality change with receding glaciers.

We will also collect measurements in the field, particularly of water quality but also soil moisture and river discharge, to inform our models and check how well they represent real conditions. A few impression of our recent field activities to collect these data can be seen here:



Recent field activities in the Santa and Vilcanota catchments to collect water quality and glacier melt data.


Our data will help us investigate how rivers and ecosystems respond to these changes and how well they can cope with further glacier loss.

title: Data and Evidence
text:
Why look back to 1850?
Scientists commonly use 1850–1900 as a reference period for measuring global warming. Industrialisation was already underway, but this period predates most human-caused warming, making it a useful baseline. It also falls near the end of the Little Ice Age, when many regions experienced cooler conditions and glaciers were living a happy life, extending their icy territory farther down mountain valleys. Disclaimer: Despite its name, this was not a full ice age, and its timing varied around the world. Volcanic eruptions, changes in the Sun’s energy, and natural climate variability contributed to the cooling.
Since this time, glaciers have receded at an accelerating pace due to global warming (Fig. 1). By looking back to 1850, we can trace key changes in river flow and the surrounding environment and investigate how they relate to glacier retreat since the end of the Little Ice Age. A long time series also helps us to detect significant shifts or tipping-points which might indicate a crucial change in hydrological behavior.

title: Data and Evidence
section: How do we generate the data?
text:
How do we generate the data?
We cannot travel back to 1850 to measure a river, but we can use evidence from the past to reconstruct how it may have behaved.
For this, we will combine historical climate data sets dating back until 1850, with reconstructions of past glacier conditions. These climate and glacier information will drive JULES - the Joint UK Land Environment Simulator. This computer model represents how water, energy, and vegetation interact. It tracks how rain and snow move through the landscape: water can remain in the soil, return to the atmosphere, or run off towards rivers.
Once the data is generated we use this data to analyse potential critical thresholds and tipping points. You can find more information on how we do this, in the Tipping Point Analysis section.

title: The Team
text:
Rike Becker (Project Lead)

I am a scientist and Marie-Skłodowska Curie Fellow at Imperial College London, studying how climate change affects glacierized mountain catchments. My research combines hydrological and land-surface models with field observations, local knowledge, satellite data, and plenty of coffee and debugging. As project lead of Tipping Rivers, I’m responsible for what you find on these pages - for better or worse. Questions, ideas and friendly feedback are always welcome at r.becker@imperial.ac.uk.
But this project is far from a solo adventure: wonderful collaborators across disciplines contribute their expertise, challenge my thinking and help untangle scientific puzzles. Thank you all!

title: Tipping Point Analysis
section: How do we find tipping points?
text:
How do we find tipping points?
Once we have simulated hydrological and environmental dynamics over the past ~180 years (1850-today), we will search for strong or abrupt changes in water availability, river flow dynamics, water quality, snow melt, soil moisture, etc. Such changes can indicate a sudden shift in water resources and a potential risk for increasing water insecurity. Four types of such potential changes are presented in the figure below.



Different types of tipping point behaviour which we will investigate in this project.


Examples for each of these are:
I. Linear change: Deviation from a reference (stable) state, causing harmful effects on the hydro-ecosystem. This could for example be a constant reduction in glacier and snow melt leading to a steady reduction in water supply and a deviation from a ‘stable’ and water secure pre-peak water state.
II. Nonlinear trends: The acceleration of a harmful effect or a change in variability leading to an unstable hydro-ecosystem outside of long-term ‘normal’ variability. For example, an increase in water temperature reaching a level which accelerates eutrophication - a lack of oxygen in water bodies which lead to dying of aquatic life.
III. Thresholds: Point of abrupt irreversible changes inhibiting a return to a previous and stable state. For example, the loss of glacier and snow melt discharge leading to the disconnection of water stores and an abrupt loss in overall river discharge (= typical tipping point behavior).
IV. Early warning signals: The shift in magnitudes and frequencies of variable dynamics. This could be a change in flow regimes due to a lack of ice and snow melt, which no longer buffers low flows during dry seasons.
The detailed identification of tipping points will be done using statistical autoregression (AR) models. With their help we will be able to assess these different types of changes in rivers and the environment. These models have been proven to be very useful in detecting small shifts in variable dynamics, which can lead to significant changes in the larger ecosystem. Here, they will be used to identify how a change in glacier melt dynamics might lead to a severe change in water quality and water quantity variables in the Vilcanota and the Santa rivers.
